summary:
Goa stands under India's national framework: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 and its March 2026 amendment operate in this state exactly as in every other state and union territory, and no Goan statute or enforcement pattern diverging from the national position is on file.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, with both houses approving it and the bill awaiting presidential assent. If assented, it removes the self-identification right established by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling in the National Legal Services Authority case, restricts legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and makes medical certification mandatory. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, amending the 2019 Act. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Critics note that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Certification under the amended regime runs through medical boards and district authorities, which must approve gender-affirming surgery. Protest against the bill was mounted in Mumbai on the day of passage.

Entry and stay sit on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Exposure for a visitor concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of a gender check; transgender people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped the openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain although she presented a PAN card. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment was drafted and passed against organised opposition: protests took place in Mumbai on 25 March 2026, and the People's Union for Civil Liberties framed the new coercion offences as a return to colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people.

Government and civil-society readings of the bill diverge. The state presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and strengthening protection from trafficking, while rights campaigners including Akkai Padmashali describe it as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist.

India's position compares unevenly with the assessment of external monitors. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 found only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, concentrated in conservative rural areas and not systemic, which sits alongside documented checkpoint incidents at railway stations, airports and passport offices in 2024 and 2026.

The trajectory of statute and of judicial protection runs in opposite directions: recognition narrowed in March 2026 and sexual-violence safeguards were removed with the 2024 criminal-code replacement, while high courts have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people, most comprehensively in the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police.
localsOnly:
Residents of Goa are governed by the same recognition machinery as the rest of India: certification runs through medical boards and district authorities, which must approve gender-affirming surgery, and legal recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex persons.

People who self-identify as trans men, trans women, gender-fluid or non-binary outside those categories have no route to legal recognition under the amended scheme, and lose the self-identification right that the 2014 Supreme Court ruling had affirmed.

Residents face the same 2024 criminal-code position as elsewhere in India: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code and removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded transgender people from sexual violence.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available to residents, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity.

Welfare-scheme access is the benefit the government advances for the amendment; the People's Union for Civil Liberties and other critics argue the scheme's definitions exclude most trans, non-binary and gender-fluid residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was not confirmed in the sources on file; the bill's operative status in Goa is therefore unresolved, and whether the coercion offence and the narrowed recognition scheme are in force is not sourced here.

No Goan enforcement record is on file: incidents of police conduct, checkpoint treatment or certification decisions specific to Goa are not sourced, and the checkpoint evidence available (Kolkata railway station, Assam Railway Protection Force custody, Chennai airport, passport authorities) comes from other Indian states.

Whether Goa's district authorities and medical boards have issued certification procedures under the amended regime is not sourced. The treatment of trans visitors holding foreign documents at Goa's own ports of entry is likewise not sourced.

The scale of the excluded population in Goa is unresolved: the two-million national estimate is not broken down by state in the material available.
